messages.body_plain:
Hi Jose,

Thanks for the tip.
I also used this one before posting.

Finally, the problem was in the constant. For the Distance sampling, all distance were in meters, and the density is in hares/km².
In the constant, I provided mid-point of each class intervals and width of distance class interval in meters, so I converted it in km but 1 value was wrong and it causes crash.

Here is the final model working :
nyears.fa <- length(unique(distance.fall$an)) # number of years
nrep.fa <- length(unique(distance.fall$num_nuit)) # number of repetition within year
npt.fa <- length(unique(distance.fall$num_pt)) # number of points for point sampling
nclass.fa <- 4  # number of distance classes
tronc <- 0.3    # truncation distance
# the guilties were here:
midpt <- c(60,150,210,270)/1000        # midpoint of each distance class
delta <- c(120,60,60,60)/1000          # width of each distance class
# providing the constants
constant.fa <- list(T = nyears.fa,
                    K = nrep.fa,
                    nsites = npt.fa,
                    nD = nclass.fa,
                    Res.cov = Res.cov, # covariate for abundance
                    area = pi*0.3*0.3,
                    light = light.cov.fa,
                    survey.N = light.cov.fa.N,
                    B = tronc,
                    midpt = midpt,        # midpoint of each distance class
                    delta = delta)          # width of each distance class

# observed data
data.fa <- list(y4d = D.data.fall,
                nobs = apply(D.data.fall,c(1,3,4),sum))

# code model DS
DS_chareil.fa <- nimbleCode({

  # Prior distributions
  beta0 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)  # Intercept for log(lambda)
  mean.lam <- exp(beta0)
  for (h in 1:2){
    beta1[h] ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
  }
  beta.trend ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)

  # phi ~ dunif(0,1)        # Probability of availability
  # # Detection parameters
  # sigma0 ~ dunif(0.1,500)   # Intercept
  # alpha2 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)   # effect of DATE (linear)
  # alpha3 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)   # effect of DATE (squared)
  # alpha4 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)   # effect of HOUR
  sigma ~ dunif(0.1,500)      # Detection function parameter
  theta ~ dunif(0.5, 5)    # Detection function parameter
  r ~ dunif(0, 10)

  # Construct the multinomial cell probabilities

  # log(g[b]) <- -midpt[b]*midpt[b]/(2*sigma*sigma) # half-normal
  cloglog(g[1:nD]) <- theta*log(sigma)  - theta*log(midpt[1:nD])  # hazard
  f[1:nD] <- (2*midpt[1:nD]*delta[1:nD])/(B*B)                # radial density function
  probs[1:nD] <- g[1:nD]*f[1:nD]
  probs.c[1:nD] <- probs[1:nD]/sum(probs[1:nD])

  for (s in 1:nsites) {
    for (k in 1:K) {
      pdet[s,k] <- sum(probs[1:nD]) # Distance class probabilities
      # pmarg[s,k] <- pdet[s,k]*phi       # Marginal probability
    }
  }

  for(t in 1:T){                        # Years
    for (s in 1:nsites) {               # Sites
      for (k in 1:K) {                  # Replicates
        # Model part 4: distance class frequencies
        y4d[s,1:nD,k,t] ~ dmulti(probs.c[1:nD], nobs[s,k,t])
        # Model part 3: total number of detections:
        nobs[s,k,t] ~ dbin(pdet[s,k], M[s,t])
        # Model part 2: Availability. Not used in this model but simulated.
        # Navail[s,k,t] ~ dbin(phi, M[s,t])
      }  # end k loop
      # Model part 1: Abundance model
      M[s,t] ~ dpois(lambda[s,t])
      log(lambda[s,t]) <- beta0 + beta1[Res.cov[s,t]] + beta.trend*(t-2.5)
    }  # end s loop
  } # end t loop

  # Derived quantities
  for(t in 1:T){
    Mtot[t] <- sum(M[1:nsites,t])
    Dtotal[t]<- Mtot[t]/(area*nsites)
    # for(k in 1:K){
    #   Ntot[k,t] <- sum(Navail[1:nsites,k,t])
    # }
  }

}
)

# inits
Navail.st <- apply(D.data.fall, c(1,3,4),sum)
# Mst <- round(matrix(M.mean,ncol = nyears.fa,nrow = npt.fa,byrow = TRUE))
Mst <- apply(Navail.st,c(1,3),max,na.rm=T) + 100
Mst[Mst=="-Inf"] <- 100
inits <- function(){
  list(M=Mst,
       # Navail = Navail.st,
       beta0 = log(2),
       beta1 = 0.5,
       sigma = 200,
       theta = 2 # ,
       ) #phi=.9
}

# create model
Rmodel <- nimbleModel(DS_chareil.fa, constant.fa, data.fa, inits = inits())
Rmodel$calculate()

# compile in C
Cmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)

# configure the model
conf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel)
conf$printMonitors()
conf$addMonitors('Mtot','Dtotal')
# conf$printSamplers(byType = TRUE)

# set MCMC
Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(conf)
Cmcmc <- compileNimble(Rmcmc, project = Cmodel)

# launch model
samples <- runMCMC(Cmcmc,200000,nburnin = 20000, nchains = 1)

# Here it goes:
> samples <- runMCMC(Cmcmc,200000,nburnin = 20000, nchains = 1)
running chain 1...
|-------------|-------------|-------------|-------------|
|----------------------------------------

So, now I'm waiting for some results and next steps will be to estimate availability.
Anyway, it was a problem with the constant data that produced wrong initial values and inconsistency in the model.

Thanks for your help !

Guillaume

> > Guillaume, thanks for your email, and your continued interest and usage of NIMBLE.

> >
> > To answer your question, no, there has not been progress on this issue of initial values with the slice sampling algorithm.  In brief, NIMBLE's MCMC (just the same as other MCMC engines) requires a "valid" starting point for the MCMC chain, manifested as a "valid" (that is, self-consistent) set of initial values for the model.  The MCMC (nor the individual sampling algorithms which comprise the MCMC, i.e., the slice sampler) is not designed nor intended to "find" a valid starting point for you.  (rather, the MCMC's goal is to *transition between* valid model states, eventually converging to the joint posterior distribution).  Point being, no, there has been no work towards an automated solution for this problem, of finding a valid initial state (a self-consistent set of model values); that it still a prerequisite of using the MCMC.
> >
> >
> >
> > All that said, if we can be of assistance and you're able to share your code and current best attempt at finding a valid starting state, then I suspect someone on this list might be able to help point out where the problem is coming from (e.g., which model value(s) are generating the inconsistencies), and help get you on the right track.

messages.subject: Re: ZIP distribution error
messages.subject_clean: ZIP distribution error
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dirk,

When I ran the above code, I reproduced the error you reported. However, when I included the construction of the rZIP random generator as in the example, the distribution registers properly. This suggests to me that there's something misaligned with the internal r-function placeholder that's used when registerDistributions is called without an available r function.

Not sure what the real problem or solution is, but hopefully this will provide a workaround for now and a starting place for others looking to debug!

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for this, Dirk.

In fact, fixing that bug was already queued up in our development branch (devel) for our next release.

Also, you no longer need to use registerDistributions for a routine case.  If you just use your distribution in a model, it will automatically detect and register it.  If there is no "r" function, it will create a placeholder.  Just be sure to provide initial values for any nodes following the new distribution so that they do not need simulated initial values, because that would require a working "r" function.

Please let us know further problems.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ollie,

Your connection to the clusters will be lost if you shut down R. That said, unless I am missing something, I don't see why you couldn't use clusterEvalQ() to return the necessary nimble objects from each cluster (such as in a list), save these nimble objects, then export the nimble objects back to individual clusters in another R session (looping clusterExport() through each cluster) and continue updating with more iterations. I am curious to see if that works, so please let me know how it goes.

I don't know about a progress bar, and the run times for each chain can be different so I don't know what one would really tell you.

Best,
Adrian

On Sun, Mar 29, 2020 at 6:55 AM orwearn <oliver...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Adrian (and all),
>
> Thanks for updating your code example. I have a follow-up query on it:
>
> Am I right in thinking that R cannot be closed between the initial run and the update in your code, because it depends on the same cluster ('cl') being open?
>
> Is there a way of saving, exiting and then updating with more iterations at a later time (as possible in runjags etc.)? (I am running NIMBLE on Google Cloud, wherein it's difficult for me to keep R open for 3+ weeks...).
>
> Many thanks for any pointers from anyone, I'm only just starting to transition over from JAGS
> Ollie
>
> PS If there's a way to add a progress bar (e.g. just for node 1), that would also be a dream...! But not to worry if that isn't possible.
>
> On Sunday, March 29, 2020 at 1:14:01 AM UTC+7, Adrian Monroe wrote:
> > Hi Ollie,
> >
> > You bring up a good point, and I am sharing this with the rest of the nimble group to clarify. It seems indeed according to chapter 7 of the nimble help (https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-mcmc.html#sec:runMCMC) that runMCMC does NOT continue an MCMC run where it left off previously. I must have missed that, and I have modified the code for sampling and updating in parallel is below. Note the update returns all iterations from the start, not just the additional samples. Interestingly, when I used runMCMC to update, it didn't look to me like it was completely starting over, but instead was sampling from distributions it had reached previously (which is probably why I assumed it picked up from the previous run). If any of the nimble developers have some insights on this, and why reset = FALSE is not the default, I would be interested.
> >
> > Best,
> > Adrian
> >
> > out1 <- clusterEvalQ(cl, {
> >   library(nimble)
> >   library(coda)
> >   model <- nimbleModel(code = myCode, name = "model",
> >                            constants = nimbleconstants, data = nimbledata,

> >   CmodelMCMC$run(10000, reset = FALSE)
> >   return(as.mcmc(as.matrix(CmodelMCMC$mvSamples)))
> > })

> > out.mcmc <- as.mcmc(out1)
> > traceplot(out.mcmc[, "b"]
> >
> > ## If has not converged, continue sampling

> > out2 <- clusterEvalQ(cl, {
> >   CmodelMCMC$run(20000, reset = FALSE)
> >   return(as.mcmc(as.matrix(CmodelMCMC$mvSamples)))
> > })
> >
> > out.mcmc.update1 <- as.mcmc(out2)
> >
> > >

Good afternoon,

I'm hoping to use RW_llFunction for regression coefficients. I have many regression coefficients and I would like to use the inprod() functionality described here: https://r-nimble.org/nimbleExamples/linpred.html

It seems that when I use RW_llFunction and I add samplers, I need to add them all as separate coeffiicients. Is there a way to add a sampler for the vector of betas? If not, it seems all betas will need to be specified manually, perhaps both in the samplers as well as in the model specification, when using RW_llFunction. Perhaps there is a way that I can use the vector in the model specification and then only have to write out all of the individual coefficients in the sampler stage?

How I currently need to implement the samplers:
mcmcConf$addSampler(target = "beta_0", type = "RW_llFunction",
                    control = list(llFunction = RllFun, includesTarget = F))
mcmcConf$addSampler(target = "beta_1", type = "RW_llFunction",
                    control = list(llFunction = RllFun, includesTarget = F))
mcmcConf$addSampler(target = "beta_2", type = "RW_llFunction",
                    control = list(llFunction = RllFun, includesTarget = F))
mcmcConf$addSampler(target = "beta_3", type = "RW_llFunction",
                    control = list(llFunction = RllFun, includesTarget = F))

How I would like to add the samplers, for example, where beta if a vector of the beta0:beta3.

messages.body_plain:
Yes, that makes sense.

I'll file an issue in our GitHub repo to check on documentation of RW_llFunction_block.

You can absolutely use the RW_llFunction[_block] route to call  a log Gaussian Cox Process likelihood.  Here is another way you could design it:

In the model, you might want e.g.

eta[1:N] ~ dLGC(params1[1:N], theta, ...[whatever parameters are needed])

You would write dLGC as a user-defined distribution (see User Manual).  If you can express the calculations you need entirely in the nimbleFunction language (what can be compiled), then your distribution will be compiled along with the rest of the model, giving fast performance.  If you need to call R, you can simply make dLGC use a nimbleRcall.  Then dLGC will be compiled via C++ but the generated C++ will issue a call to R for the nimbleRcall.  Any step into R will impose a performance penalty but gives you a lot of flexibility.  Doing it either of these ways would allow you to stay within default sampler assignments, or to customize samplers more flexibly.  With the external llFunction samplers, we just have the two options, RW and RW block (both Metropolis-Hastings).

Does that make sense?

-Perry

messages.subject_clean: Efficient Data Augmentation for ZIP models
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to fit ZIP models in NIMBLE using data augmentation. For example,

nimbleCode({
  beta0 ~ dflat()
  tau ~ dgamma(0.001, 0.001)
  p ~dunif(0,1)
  psi[1:N] ~ dcar_normal(adj[1:L], weights[1:L], num[1:N], tau, zero_mean = 1)
  for(i in 1:N) {
    S[i] ~ dbern(p)
    mu[i] <- exp(log(E[i])+beta0 + psi[i])*(1-S[i]) +.001
    y[i] ~ dpois(mu[i])
  }
})

A disease mapping example. It works without issue but I plan to extend it to to a large data set and would like to make it more efficient. I know that S[i] can not be 1 when y[i]>0 so you only need to sample S[i] when y[i]=0. I am not sure the best way to implement this in Nimble. I know I can put S[i] to 0 in the model code but I would rather not do that since I think the model is written properly right now. I read about custom samplers but that seems like overkill. I just want S[i] to always to be 0 when y[i]>0.

Also the full conditional probability S[i]=1 has a simple form p/(p+(1-p)exp(-mu[i])). I do not know if it is worth simplifying it or not using a custom sampler or if Nimble simplifies it like this.

Thanks!

so maybe instead of S[i]~dbern(p) you could do...

Something like that might do the trick.

-Heather

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for that suggestion, Heather.

Another way, which is used in other contexts, is to provide some S[i] values as data.  For i such that y[i] > 0, provide S[i] = 0 as data.  For other i, set S[i] to NA in the data vector you provide.  Those elements will be sampled by the MCMC.

This is also done in capture-recapture models in ecology.  When a capture history is 1 0 1 0 0 (1 = alive, 0 = dead, the sequence is over capture occasions through time), the latent state of whether the animal is alive or dead is known to be alive for the first three times but unknown for the last two times (after the last live capture).

-Perry

})

messages.subject: Storing eigecomponents in nimble
messages.subject_clean: Storing eigecomponents in nimble
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to embed an eigendecomposition of a fixed n x n matrix (Sigma) within my nimble model string. The goal is to compute the eigenvectors and values of the matrix at each iteration of an MCMC algorithm. My nimble model builds properly when I perform two separate eigendecompositions of the same n x n matrix. That is, one to extract the eigenvectors and another for the eigenvalues.

In order to manage the computational costs, is it possible to run just one eigendecomposition and store both eigencomponents in a nimbleList or an eigenNimbleList?  Though the help manual provides some related code (Section 13.2.1 - Using eigen and svd in nimbleFunctions), I haven't been able to successfully apply this to the problem at hand. Any tips or pointers would be much appreciated!

Attached, please find the toy example R file, and the pertinent model string is as follows:

model_string <- nimbleCode({

  # Data Model - Poisson Likelihood
  for(i in 1:n){
    Z[i] ~ dpois(lambda = lambda[i])
    lambda[i] <- exp(W[i]+XB[i])
  }

  XB[1:n]<-beta1*X[,1] + beta2*X[,2]

  # Process Model
  W[1:n] <- U[1:n,1:n]%*%(D[1:n,1:n]%*%delta[1:n])

  # Currently requires two eigendecompositions of the n x n matrix Sigma (Sigma is fixed in the toy example)
  # Is it possible to perform on eigendecomposition and store the eigenvectors and eigenvalues in a single object
  U[1:n,1:n]  <- eigen(Sigma[1:n,1:n], symmetric = TRUE)$vectors[1:n,1:n]
  D[1:n,1:n] <- diag(sqrt(eigen(Sigma[1:n,1:n], symmetric = TRUE)$values[1:n]))

  for(i in 1:n) {
    delta[i] ~ dnorm(mean=0,  var=1)
  }

  # Parameter Model
  beta1 ~  dnorm(0, sd=sqrt(100))
  beta2 ~  dnorm(0, sd=sqrt(100))
})

Thank you very much!

Best,
Ben

messages.body_plain:
To add just a few things:

1) I'm not sure if there's any way to have the progress bar printed from one cluster node.  I agree, that would be nice.

2) Even if you return the compiled object(s) from one cluster (looping over clusterExport(), as was suggested), these compiled objects still could not be saved (to be reloaded subsequently into a new R session) due to the current nature of NIMBLE's compilation and the resulting objects.  As I believe was mentioned, addressing this is a long-term goal for NIMBLE.

3) Towards that end - being able to start a new R session, and resume executing an MCMC chain precisely where it left off - I wrote a vignette about "Saving Model and MCMC State", which demonstrates how to save the model and MCMC state after executing an MCMC algorithm.  This is only demonstrated for a single chain, but could be generalized for the multi-chain case.  See the vignette here:
https://danielturek.github.io/public/saveMCMCstate/saveMCMCstate.html

Hope this helps!
Daniel

The graph defined by this model seems to have cycles.

Here is an example:

phi.off[32] -> phi.mu <http://phi.mu>[11] -> phi[11] -> phi.off[1] -> phi.mu <http://phi.mu>[1] -> phi[1] -> phi.off[14] -> phi.off[32]

where "a -> b" means b depends on a.

There are lots of others, mostly longer.

I'm not sure what is going on, but that is the proximate reason for the error.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Diego, to follow up on the general issue here.

1) Nimble (JAGS as well) does not allow for cycles. So to specify a CAR model in nimble you must specify the joint distribution for all the random effects as a vector (please see the manual chapter on CAR models). The specification in Nimble is similar to the dcar specifications in GeoBUGS.

2) I don't see in the GeoBUGS documentation that cycles are allowed, but given that MacNab et al. (2006) have such BUGS code with cycles and that the BUGS manual does not say cycles are not allowed, presumably it is possible. Here is a post  <https://sourceforge.net/p/mcmc-jags/discussion/610036/thread/060dacfb/?limit=25>on the JAGS mailing list in which this is discussed. Note that in the post, Martyn Plummer (the JAGS developer)  cautions the user that just because an MCMC runs in (Open)BUGS doesn't mean the MCMC is valid (in particular the issue he is concerned with is whether the conditional distributions specified give a coherent joint distribution). I would suspect that if the conditionals are correctly specified the MCMC output from BUGS would be valid.

Chris

messages.subject: Re: Storing eigecomponents in nimble
messages.subject_clean: Storing eigecomponents in nimble
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

Good question. It's not directly possible in model code because one can't use a list or other complicated data structure in model code. However you can do it by writing a user-defined function. This user defined function would compute the eigendecomposition and return the result as a (n x (n+1)) or ((n+1) x n) matrix, where the extra column or row contains the eigenvalues. You would then use subsets of this matrix appropriately in your model code.

Your model code would look something like this:

W[1:n] <- (U[1:n,1:n]%*%(sqrt(U[1:n,n+1])*delta[1:n]))[ , 1]
U[1:n, 1:(n+1)] <- myEigenDecomp(Sigma[1:n, 1:n])

where `myEigenDecomp` is a user-defined function. For more info on writing a user-defined function you can look in the manual. For an example of a user-defined function, please see: https://r-nimble.org/nimbleExamples/gaussian_process.html. The latter plus the material in Sec. 13.2.1 that you've already seen may be sufficient for you.

Side note: You need the [,1] at the end because the result of the matrix multiplication is a (one-column) matrix and to assign to a vector you need to "subset" it.

messages.subject: Re: Storing eigecomponents in nimble
messages.subject_clean: Storing eigecomponents in nimble
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

Thank you so much for taking a look at this. I followed your suggestion, and it seems to have done the trick!

I basically created a user-defined function (outside of the model code) that returns a matrix comprised of the eigenvectors and eigenvalues (last column). Then I embedded it into the model code as you advised. Thank you again.

The user-defined function and model code is:

eigDecomp<-nimbleFunction(
  run = function(sigma = double(2)) {
    returnType(double(2))
    n=dim(sigma)[1]
    result<-matrix(nrow = n, ncol = n+1, init = FALSE)
    eigFull <- eigen(sigma,symmetric = TRUE)
    result[1:n,1:n]<-eigFull$vectors[1:n,1:n]
    result[1:n,n+1]<-eigFull$values[1:n]
    return(result)
  })

# Nimble Model

model_string <- nimbleCode({

  # Data Model - Poisson Likelihood
  for(i in 1:n){
    Z[i] ~ dpois(lambda = lambda[i])
    lambda[i] <- exp(W[i]+XB[i])
  }

  XB[1:n]<-beta1*X[,1] + beta2*X[,2]

  # Process Model

  W[1:n] <- (U[1:n,1:n]%*%(sqrt(U[1:n,n+1])*delta[1:n]))[ , 1]

  U[1:n, 1:(n+1)] <- eigDecomp(Sigma[1:n, 1:n])

  for(i in 1:n) {
    delta[i] ~ dnorm(mean=0,  var=1)
  }

  # Parameter Model
  beta1 ~  dnorm(0, sd=sqrt(100))
  beta2 ~  dnorm(0, sd=sqrt(100))
})

Best,
Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am using nimble to run the Spatial Count model (Royle, Chandler SCR Book, spatial model to estimate species abundance/density from camera counts).  I am evaluating the detection portion with a linear predictor with 2 covariates and an interaction term:

Log(lamda0) = beta0 + beta[1]* snow + beta[2]*temperature + beta[3] * snow * temperature

I am using reversible jump mcmc to do model selection and my question is a about how to implement this with the interaction term. I am using indicator variable and have experimented using reversible jump a couple of ways:

1. single indicator for the interaction..

Log(lamda0) = beta0 + indicator[1]* beta[1]* snow + indicator[2]* beta[2]*temperature

+ indicator[3]* beta[3] * snow * temperature

2. combined indicators for the interaction..

Log(lamda0) = beta0 + indicator[1]* beta[1]* snow + indicator[2]* beta[2]*temperature

          + indicator[1]* indicator[2]* indicator[3]* beta[3] * snow * temperature

Both of these models run and give surprisingly similar results in my testing, but I am not sure if either one is appropriate.  I have hunted around the web/literature a bit but have not found a clear answer.

One follow up question, in my tests (both cases above, run on coyote data from a camera trap array), I get pretty low numbers for the indicator posterior means (like .18 for the interaction, and really low for the individual covariates (around .01 to .001).  Are these numbers simply suggesting that there is not much support for the covariates in the model (in other words support for the dot model), or should the indicator means be interpreted relative to each other?  I don’t think that a reproducible example is needed here, but please let me know if anyone thinks otherwise and I could try to supply something.

Thank you.

Brian

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am trying to build an observation model for Covid19 in Norway to estimate the unobserved number of infected individuals.

To estimate the growth rate of the epidemic I am using a semi-mechanistic approach. The infected individuals on day "i" is calculated as the sum of the infected individuals on all the previous days, times the discretized serial interval evaluated at the difference in days. To store this sum I need to loop over all the previous indexes for each value of i. The sum on the last day is multiplied with the growth rate to obtain the prediction for the next day.

However, for some reason, I am unable to configure the model when I try to use the last column index of the variable "store_sum". The error happens after the model is defined and I use the command "configureMCMC(MOD1, monitors = monitor,thin=1e1)".  I don't get any error messages, R just goes into an infinite calculation and I have to force quit the application to continue.
The model works fine if I use index i-1 in the sum instead.
Why doesn't configureMCMC work when I try to use the last index of my sum? It should be well defined by indexes provided in my loops. Am I confusing Nimble through the way I specify the dimensions?

A reproducible example is provided below.
Any help greatly appreciated.

Best regards,
Magnus Nygård Osnes

library(nimble)
chooseR = c(rep(1,18), rep(0,22))
constant_list = list(N0 = 6, Nend =41,chooseR= chooseR)

#THIS WORKS

mod_test = nimbleCode({
  m ~ dgamma(0.5,1)
  Rt <- mu #Growth rate
  Rm <- mu*exp(-m) #reduced growth rate
  tau <- 5.72

  ym ~ dexp(1.0/tau) #Seed the beginning of the epidemic.
  prediction[1:N0] <- ym #Learn infected 6 first days

  for (i in (N0+1):Nend) {
    store_sum[i-N0,1]<-0
    for(j in 2:i) {
      store_sum[i-N0,j] <- store_sum[i-N0,j-1]+prediction[j-1]
    }
    contribution[i] <- store_sum[i-N0,i-1]
    prediction[i] <- Rt*(chooseR[i])*contribution[i] + Rm*(1-chooseR[i])*contribution[i]
  }
})

test_inits = function() {
  mu = 2.4
  tau = 5.72
  ym = 1/tau
  m = 1
  list(mu = mu,tau=tau,ym=ym,m=m)
}

MOD1 <- nimbleModel(mod_test,constants = constant_list,inits =test_inits())
monitor <- c("store_sum", "contribution")
mcmcConf <- configureMCMC(MOD1, monitors = monitor,thin=1e1)

#THIS DOESN'T WORK: The only difference is: contribution[i] <- store_sum[i-N0,i], instead of contribution[i] <- store_sum[i-N0,i-1].

mod_test = nimbleCode({
  m ~ dgamma(0.5,1)
  Rt <- mu #Growth rate
  Rm <- mu*exp(-m) #reduced growth rate
  tau <- 5.72

  ym ~ dexp(1.0/tau) #Seed the beginning of the epidemic.
  prediction[1:N0] <- ym #Learn infected 6 first days

  for (i in (N0+1):Nend) {
    store_sum[i-N0,1]<-0
    for(j in 2:i) {
      store_sum[i-N0,j] <- store_sum[i-N0,j-1]+prediction[j-1]
    }
    contribution[i] <- store_sum[i-N0,i]
    prediction[i] <- Rt*(chooseR[i])*contribution[i] + Rm*(1-chooseR[i])*contribution[i]
  }
})

test_inits = function() {
  mu = 2.4
  tau = 5.72
  ym = 1/tau
  m = 1
  list(mu = mu,tau=tau,ym=ym,m=m)
}

MOD1 <- nimbleModel(mod_test,constants = constant_list,inits =test_inits())
monitor <- c("store_sum", "contribution")
mcmcConf <- configureMCMC(MOD1, monitors = monitor,thin=1e1)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Magnus,

Thanks for posting your question.

I haven't tracked down why the second case goes into possibly infinite recursion, but a workaround is to include "useConjugacy = FALSE" in configureMCMC.  Determination of conjugate relationships for sampling involves tracing algebraic relationships through deterministic nodes.  With very long sequences of deterministic dependencies, this can get bogged down.  In this case it might be a bug.

A couple of other points I noticed: If I follow, it looks like chooseR should be one element longer.  And there are no data in the model, so ym will just follow its prior.  I realize you might still be building up the ideas.

If the very many deterministic dependencies in this model become cumbersome, you could do all of the store_sum and contribution work in a user-defined function.

Let us know further questions.

-Perry

messages.subject_clean: Reversible jump mcmc with an interaction term
messages.body_plain:
Hi Brian,

sorry for the late reply on this. I think that option 2 makes sense, interaction should be in the model if both main effects are. The drawback of option 2 is that the interaction coefficient would be sampled even when it is not in the model.  To prevent this, I'd suggest you to use dconstraint. In this way you can force indicator[3] to be equal to 1 only when both the main effects are in the model. In model code

constraint ~ dconstraint(indicator[1] >= indicator[3] & indicator[2] >= indicator[3])

Log(lamda0) = beta0 + indicator[1]* beta[1]* snow + indicator[2]* beta[2]*temperature
+ indicator[3]* beta[3] * snow * temperature

and you can set the value of constraint in the data, i.e. data$constraint = 1. If the condition is violated, the likelihood for dconstraint is zero, which is used whenever a change to any of indicator[1], indicator[2], indicator[3] is proposed.

Make sure to initialize the model with values that satisfy the constraint. This should help to adjust inclusion probabilities.  Note also that with this constraint, the RJMCMC would not remove a main effect unless all of its interactions are out of the model, which may result in slow mixing. Feel free to follow up on this!

Best,

Sally

Hello everyone!

I am working on a project where I would like to define my own distribution and use MCMC through NIMBLE. I heard NIMBLE allowed one to create user defined distributions, as long as I had the pdf and a way to sample from it. However, when I read through the manual on the topic, the example given gave the exponential distribution, which has a nice closed form solution if one wants to use inverse transform sampling. The distribution I want to use (which models the behavior of the p-value in a one sample z-test) probably does not have a closed form inverse cdf, since part of the distribution involves the quantile function of the normal distribution. Are there examples out there of users using other methods (such as accept reject sampling) or using a non-closed form representation of the inverse cdf of a user defined distribution in order to do MCMC in NIMBLE?

Thanks a million! Good luck out there with all the virus stuff. Hope ya'll are staying safe and healthy.

messages.body_plain:
hi Matt,

If the algorithm you'll be using doesn't simulate from the distributions (this is true of NIMBLE's built-in MCMC samplers) then you only need to define the density ('d') function and not the random generation ('r') function. Our documentation on this point has been a bit inconsistent/confusing -- we're trying to clean things up on that front (and please email me separately if you have noticed any confusing documentation that led to your email). So you may not need to write the function to do sampling. If that's the case, just write the 'd' function and then use the distribution in your model code. It should just work.

If the algorithm you'll use does need the 'r' function, you can use any of the functionality documented for writing nimbleFunctions in your 'r' function, including looping and qnorm().  Others may have examples they can share.

Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Matt,

I was about to reply as well, so let me add to Chris' reply.  It's true that nimble allows you to write new distributions and also to write new samplers, but these are separate features.  Your email makes it sound like you might be under the impression that you can only add a distribution if you also have the wherewithal to provide a sampler, but that is not the case.  If you can provide the "d" function for your distribution, you can typically let nimble's built-in samplers take it from there.  For a univariate continuous distribution, the default sampler will be an adaptive random-walk Metropolis-Hastings sampler.

I hope that helps.  Let us know further questions.

-Perry

messages.subject_clean: Nimble error with Nimble 0.9 but not with 0.7.1
messages.body_plain:
Hi Pierre,

Thanks for reporting this. In a recent version of nimble we introduced
some checking to warn users of how to set up their model for improved
computational efficiency. It turns out that the checking we (well,
actually me!) introduced was not sophisticated enough to handle the
somewhat complicated indexing your model is using.

We'll fix this in our next release (coming in a month or two), but for
now, if you'd like you can install off of a branch on Github that has
the fix.

devtools::install_github(repo="nimble-dev/nimble/packages/nimble",
ref="issue_996")

A couple side notes about your model:
1) When you try your code in the version of nimble that has the fix,
it will warn you about computational efficiency. In your case, since
tabfin[,1], tabfin[,2] and tabfin[,4] never change, it's best to
provide them to nimbleModel() as constants and have tabfin[,3] as a
separate variable provided as data. If they are not provided as
constants, nimble will think that their values might change during an
algorithm, and this causes a lot of unnecessary computation because
the dependency structure of the graphical model could in principle
change. Similarly you will probably want Q to be provided as a
constant.

2) I noticed that for some of your observations, the Poisson mean is
negative (e.g. for observation number 301) for the values that you
provided in your example.

chris

Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Brian,

My first guess is that there might be an initialization issue.  Are you providing a complete set of inits, including all latent random variables?  Because the issue likely involves the data, constants and inits, we would need a fully reproducible example to examine further.  You can send these off-list if you prefer and we can reply on-list for interested followers.

Here is an example of the kind of problem that could arise.  If the initial values for the various etas and/or omegas (which I can't see defined), happen to make a Poisson parameter or a binomial prob parameter negative, there would be no valid MCMC update.  More subtly, even if one of those parameters is 0, then if the initial value of the declared random variable is non-zero, the model will be initialized with impossible values, giving an initial total log probability of -Inf, making it likely the MCMC will go off the rails.  After building the model, you can inspect it as described in the user manual to see where there may be problematic initial values.  For example,

model$calculate() ## see if the initial log prob of the entire model is -Inf
model$calculate("N[1, 1:10]") ## check log probs of particular part of the model
model$getParam("N[1, 5]", "lambda") ## check what is calculated for this Poisson parameter.
model$eta.BSalpha ## check values in the model

Some other examples of inspecting models can be found in previous nimble-users messages.

Best,
Perry

messages.subject: Occupancy model convergence issues
messages.subject_clean: Occupancy model convergence issues
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I'm trying to get an occupancy model for a large dataset to converge and am running into memory usage issues. I can't run the chains for enough iterations to achieve convergence without getting an error along the lines of "Can't allocate vector of size X GB".  I was wondering if anyone had any suggestions, whether it's increasing sampling efficiency or reducing the amount of memory used.

Thank you in advance!

Kelley

I have included the model code below, along with some details about the size of the data.

code <- nimbleCode({

    #Estimate psi for each site
    for (i in 1:nsites) {
        logit(psi[i]) <- alpha0 + beta*X1[i] + gamma*X2[i] + delta*X3[i]
        z[i] ~ dbern(psi[i])
    }

    #Estimate p for each observation
    for (j in 1:nsites.visits) {
        logit(p[j]) <- obs[IDobs[j]] + zeta*Y1[j] + eta*Y2[j] + mos[IDmos[j]] + yr[IDyr[j]]
        p.temp[j]  <- z[Site[j]] * p[j]
        h[j] ~ dbern(p.temp[j])
    }

    #Priors
    alpha0 ~ dunif(-5, 5) #intercept for occupancy
    beta ~ dunif(-5, 5) # occupancy coefficient associated with population density
    gamma ~ dunif(-5, 5) #occupancy coefficient associated with temperature
    delta ~ dunif(-5, 5) # occupancy coefficient associated with area
    zeta ~ dunif(-5, 5) # detection coefficient associated with whether collector has previously collected the species
    eta ~ dunif(-5, 5) # detection coefficient associated with whether collector is a citizen scientist

    #Random effect of collector
    for(j in 1:nobs) {
      obs[j] ~ dnorm(0, tau=tauobs)
    }

    #Random effect of month
    for(k in 1:nmos){
      mos[k] ~ dnorm(0, tau=taumos)
    }

    #Random effect of year
    for(l in 1:nyr){
      yr[l] ~ dnorm(0, tau=tauyr)
    }

    #Hyperpriors
    tauobs ~ dgamma(0.01, 0.01)
    taumos ~ dgamma(0.01, 0.01)
    tauyr  ~ dgamma(0.01, 0.01)

    #Derived parameter
    N <- sum(z[])
})

monitors <- c("N","psi",  "p", "alpha0","beta", "gamma", "delta", "zeta",
                   "eta", "obs", "mos", "yr", "tauobs",
                   "taumos", "tauyr") # parameters to monitor

#N: the number of sites occupied (1 value)
#psi: Occupancy (67 values)
#p: Detection probability (24240 values, one for each site visit)
#alpha0: Occupancy intercept (1 value)
#beta: occupancy coefficient (1 value)
#gamma: occupancy coefficient (1 value)
#delta: occupancy coefficient (1 value)
#zeta: detection coefficient (1 value)
#eta: detection coefficient (1 value)
#obs: random effect of collector (762 values)
#mos: random effect of month (12 values)
#yr: random effect of year (124 values)
#tauobs: hyperprior associated with random effect of collector
#taumos: hyperprior associated with random effect of month
#tauyr: hyperprior associated with random effect of year

initsFx <- function() {

    list(

      z = rep(1, nsites),
        beta = rnorm(1),
        gamma = rnorm(1),
        delta = rnorm(1),
        zeta = rnorm(1),
        eta = rnorm(1),
        alpha0 = rnorm(1),
        obs = rnorm(nobs),
        mos = rnorm(nmos),
        yr = rnorm(nyr),
        tauobs = rlnorm(1),
        taumos = rlnorm(1),
        tauyr = rlnorm(1)
    )
}

nimbleOptions(clearNimbleFunctionsAfterCompiling=T)
mcmc1 <- nimbleMCMC(
    code = code, constants = constants, data = data,
    monitors = monitors, inits = initsFx,
    nchains = 1, niter = 102686, nburnin = 1000, thin = 1,
    summary = T, WAIC = F, samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE
)

messages.subject: Re: Occupancy model convergence issues
messages.subject_clean: Occupancy model convergence issues
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kelley,

Thanks for the question.

It looks like you are trying to monitor 25215 parameters for 102686 iterations.  That's about 2.6 billion numbers.  Each double-precision number is 8 bytes, and a gigabyte is 2^30 bytes.  Putting it together, it looks like you are requesting 19.3 gigabytes in MCMC output.  Sometimes nimble gets into other kinds of memory use issues, but in this case I think you'll want to reduce what you are requesting from the MCMC.  Options would include thinning, not monitoring p, or using the monitor2/thin2 system to monitor p at much higher thinning than the other parameters.  To use monitors2/thin2, you'll have to switch to building the model and MCMC yourself.  It would look like:

m <- nimbleModel(code = code, constants = constants, data = data, inits = initsFx)
MCMC <- buildMCMC(m, monitors = monitors, monitors2 = monitors2) ## take "p" out of monitors and put it in monitors2
comp <- compileNimble(m, MCMC)
samples <- runMCMC(comp$MCMC, niter = 100000, nburnin = 1000, thin = 1, thin2 = 100, summary = TRUE, WAIC = FALSE, samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE)

-Perry

messages.subject: nimbleEcology: custom NIMBLE distributions for ecologists
messages.subject_clean: nimbleEcology: custom NIMBLE distributions for ecologists
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'd like to advertise an auxiliary NIMBLE package, nimbleEcology.

nimbleEcology contains a set of distributions corresponding to some common ecological models. These distributions are implemented to integrate over latent states in the model. It's designed to integrate smoothly with NIMBLE model coding.

The following distributions are available:
dOcc  (occupancy model)
dDynOcc  (dynamic occupancy model)
dHMM  (hidden Markov model)
dDHMM  (dynamic hidden Markov model)
dCJS  (Cormack-Jolly-Seber or mark-recapture model)
dNmixture  (N-mixture model)
nimbleEcology and its documentation are now available on CRAN <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/nimbleEcology/index.html> and GitHub <https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimbleEcology>. It was also discussed in the recent Ecol & Evol paper "One size does not fit all: Customizing MCMC methods for hierarchical models using NIMBLE" (Ponisio et al., 2020 <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ece3.6053>). See also this blog post <https://r-nimble.org/nimbleecology-custom-nimble-distributions-for-ecologists> with example code on r-nimble.org <http://r-nimble.org>.

Thanks,
Ben Goldstein

HI Kelley,
I've run into this problem a lot, since I work with extremely large datasets as well. It gets especially bad when you are fitting multi-species models.

My number 1 solution is to save only the stochastic nodes that bear on the value you need to know (i.e., the coefficients, the z values, and the random effect values). If you know these values, you can calculate psi and p for each iteration after the fact.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dirk, we  don't support the use of a vector as a set of indices in model code, which is how you are using 'adj' here. In other words, we are expecting code like: `sum(y[2:5])` or   `sum(y[idx[1]:idx[4]])` not `sum(y[idx[1:4]])`.
The error message you are getting here is misleading; I'll file an issue for us to look at improving that.

In terms of how to work around this, a couple options that occur to me (others might have other suggestions):

1) if Snei0 is not used elsewhere in the model (i.e., if it is just a posterior functional you need), you may want to just do the calculation with the posterior samples outside of the model.

2) You could write a user-defined function that takes 'adj', 'S0', 'count' as inputs and does the calculation within the function. I think this will work but haven't tested it:

mysum <- nimbleFunction(
    run = function(S0 = double(1), adj = double(1), count = double(1), num = double(1), i = double(0)) {
        return(sum(S0[adj[count[i]:(count[i]+num[i]-1)]])
        returnType(double(0))
    }
)

Then in model code:

Snei0[i] <- mysum(S0, adj, count, num, i)

-Chris

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Guanyu for providing this link:
https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/
I am not certain but I think the need for a manual step to modify path was a change at some point.  It used to be an installation option.

My link to the previous nimble-users exchange did not work.  Here is the summary list from those messages:

Windows:
1. Be sure to check box to set PATH when installing Rtools.exe.  Atlernatively, set PATH manually using Diba's tip.
2. Be sure Rtools.exe version matches R version.
3. We have seen some problems resolved by re-installing Rtools followed by re-installing nimble.
4. Sometimes R might need to be run as administrator to have appropriate permissions.  (Does anyone have any insight into when this is relevant for nimble?)
5. If there are filesystem or permissions issues, it is possible to install nimble in a local directory.
6. At some point in the past, Windows users reported problems if their file system involved a space in a directory name in the path to RHOME.  I think we have this resolved, so we would be interested if anyone has experience on this.
7. At some point in the past, perhaps for same reason as #6, Windows users reported problems if R is installed on a network drive.  Does anyone have recent experience with this?
8. If problems arise from generating and compiling C++ files in R's tempdir(), one can use the dirName argument to compileNimble to put such files elsewhere, such as in a local work directory.  I think this shouldn't be necessary since tempdir() should be somewhere with write permission, but does anyone know more about this on Windows?

OS X:
1. Newly installed Xcode or command line tools may need to be started once manually to provide a one-time permission before they will work from nimble.
2. If multiple C++ compilers are present on a system, be sure the PATH will find the right one.

However this gave the following error when using nimbleModel:

ab=cumNSC2[i]+1

messages.body_plain:
Christel, basically the functionality you're looking for is model$setData(newDataList).  If you do this using the compiled model object (Cmodel), then the compiledMCMC will operate using the newDataList.  A very simple example is given below.

library(nimble)

N <- 10
y.first <- 1:N

code <- nimbleCode({
    mu ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1000)
    sigma ~ dunif(0, 1000)
    for(i in 1:N) {
        y[i] ~ dnorm(mu, sd = sigma)
    }
})
constants <- list(N = N)
data <- list(y = y.first)
inits <- list(mu = 0, sigma = 1)

Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code, constants, data, inits)
Rmodel$calculate()

conf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel)
Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(conf)
Cmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)
Cmcmc <- compileNimble(Rmcmc, project = Rmodel)

samples.first <- runMCMC(Cmcmc, 10000)
samplesSummary(samples.first)

y.second <- 2*(1:N)
Cmodel$setData(y = y.second)

samples.second <- runMCMC(Cmcmc, 10000)
samplesSummary(samples.second)

So the igraph installation is failing. This is unrelated to nimble, but igraph does need to be installed for nimble to be installed.

I suspect you have an old version of gcc.  You could check with the administrator of your server if a newer version is available (or could be made available) on the system and use that.
Alternatively, as discussed here <https://github.com/igraph/rigraph/issues/338>, you could install an old version of igraph and then install nimble.

It looks like something went haywire with the nimbleOptions suggestion.

I'm not sure what's wrong.  Your code works for me.  If I enter "nimbleOptions(showCompilerOutput = TRUE)" first, it also works (and shows C++ compiler output, which is not pretty).

Brett's point is good: It is always slightly hazardous to rely on an argument that is itself an assignment expression.  Since R uses lazy evaluation, the assignment won't be evaluated until the argument is needed inside the function.  But often it works out ok, and in this case it seemed to be ok.

Oh, from your most recent message I see a confusion.

nimbleOptions(showCompilerOutput = TRUE)

should be its own line, not an argument to compileNimble.  (Actually, an alternative is to use "showCompilerOutput = TRUE" as an argument to compileNimble.)

I think this will get us back on track to look at your C++ configuration problem.

-Perry

messages.subject: RE: Summing a parameter vector across neighbors
messages.subject_clean: Summing a parameter vector across neighbors
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris

There seems to be some different issues with the summing of neighbors.

Some background:

The Leroux model if specified via the conditional mean and variance

has a sum of random effect values across neighbors. The original BUGS code that impemented this is given in

MacNab et al (2006) (attached). Also the code appears in Peter Congdon's book: Applied Bayesian Hierarchical Methods (2010)

below is the code in BUGS format: s[] is the effect and cumNSC2 is the index to neighbors vector:

##################################################################

model

{for (i in 1:m){Y1998[i]~dpois(mu[i])

p.sig[i]<-step(s[i])

log(mu[i])<-log(Exp98[i])+log(theta[i])

log(theta[i])<-a0+s[i]

s[i]~dnorm(S[i],tau[i])

tau[i]<-inv.delta*(1-lam+lam*num[i])

S[i]<-(lam/(1-lam+lam*num[i]))*sum(Ws[cumNSC2[i]+1:cumNSC2[i+1]])}

for (i in 1:sumNumNeigh){Ws[i]<-s[adj[i]]}

inv.delta~dgamma(2,0.5)

a0~dnorm(0,tau0)

tau0~dgamma(2,0.5)

lam~dunif(0,1)

}

#####################################################################

Alternative formulations in nimble could be imagined I guess: where the covariance is directly modelled.

There are other situations where a sum over neighbors is used in spatial or spatial -temporal models

For instance, with infectious disease models it is often reasonable to assume that transmission

occurs across neighbor boundaries from infectives arising in a previous time period. It is normal in these tyoes of models to

model the dependence on previous counts rather than on an evolving mean level.

Some code below is from a SIR model with this included, where case is the infective count and cumN is the index to the neighbors.

#####################################################################

for (i in 1:n) {

lsum[i,1]<-sum(wec[cumN[i]+1:cumN[i+1],1])

case[i,1]~dpois(mean[i,1])

log(mean[i,1])<-log(pop[i,1])+int0

for(j  in 2:T)

{

lsum[i,j]<-sum(wec[cumN[i]+1:cumN[i+1],j-1])

case[i,j]~dpois(mean[i,j])

log(mean[i,j])<-log(pop[i,j])+a0+

a_case*log(case[i,j-1]+0.0001)+

a_lsum*log(lsum[i,j]+0.001)

}

## and below the wec vector is set up:

for(k in 1:sumNumNeigh){

for (j in 1:13){

wec[k,j]<-case[adj[k],j]

}}

#################################################################

Of course in this case the lsum matrix can be pre-computed, and this would save

on computation.

I have implemented this pre-computation for nimble and this works. However I

havent as yet fixed the direct coded version.

BTW one small issue I have had with using nimble for these SIR models is that

when monitoring nodes it appears that the outcome data is regarded as a stochastic node and

reported in output. There is no missingness in the outcomes BTW.

I guess it is something to do with the fact we are using some pieces of the data

as conditional on others.

best

Whoops, in my email to Dirk, I forgot to give indices for the inputs to mysum. So in response to both your emails, it would be like this:

Snei0[i] <- mysum(S0[1:N1], adj[1:N2], count[1:N3], num[1:N4], i)

(The N1, N2, N3, and N4 are just placeholders, replace each with the appropriate length of the corresponding vector, either as a fixed number of a number provided via 'constants'.)

Andrew, I hadn't realized BUGS allowed something like "x[adj[1:3]]".  Is there a published example or BUGS documentation that gives an example of this we could look at?

messages.body_plain:
Hello Perry,

Thank you very much for your response. I appreciate your suggestion about creating a user-defined distribution and I think this may be helpful.

After reading the manual, it seems that to create a user-defined distribution, you need both a density (d) function and a simulation (r) function. I think the density function is rather straightforward as I already have to define the likelihood for the RW_llFunction sampler. I think the r function is slightly less intuitive for LGCP's, but perhaps you have some ideas or I'm thinking about it incorrectly. The manual suggests that you need to specify n, but n itself is random with LGCP's. I suppose we could generate n and then simulate an LGCP given n. Also, the output of a simulation from LGCP's would be a set of locations. Do you think this is possible under the user-defined distribution? Where is the r function used in sampling and why is it necessary?

Thank you again for your time!

Best,
Claire

On Wednesday, April 1, 2020 at 4:06:11 PM UTC-4, pdevalpine wrote:

> Yes, that makes sense.
>
> I'll file an issue in our GitHub repo to check on documentation of RW_llFunction_block.
>
> You can absolutely use the RW_llFunction[_block] route to call  a log Gaussian Cox Process likelihood.  Here is another way you could design it:
>
> In the model, you might want e.g.
>
> eta[1:N] ~ dLGC(params1[1:N], theta, ...[whatever parameters are needed])
>
> You would write dLGC as a user-defined distribution (see User Manual).  If you can express the calculations you need entirely in the nimbleFunction language (what can be compiled), then your distribution will be compiled along with the rest of the model, giving fast performance.  If you need to call R, you can simply make dLGC use a nimbleRcall.  Then dLGC will be compiled via C++ but the generated C++ will issue a call to R for the nimbleRcall.  Any step into R will impose a performance penalty but gives you a lot of flexibility.  Doing it either of these ways would allow you to stay within default sampler assignments, or to customize samplers more flexibly.  With the external llFunction samplers, we just have the two options, RW and RW block (both Metropolis-Hastings).
>
> Does that make sense?
>
> -Perry
>

Hi Claire,

You only need to provide the "r" function if an algorithm will need to use it.  For the case of MCMC, if you provide initial values (inits) for the LGCP, then the MCMC will not try to initialize it by drawing from its r function, and the MCMC samplers do not (typically) use the r function, so it should be ok to go without an r function.  You may see a warning message that you can ignore.

-Perry

set.seed(0820)

nimbleOptions(showCompilerOutput = TRUE)
model_string <- nimbleCode({
  for(i in 1:n){
    mass[i] ~ dnorm(mn[i],tau)
    mn[i]  <- beta1 + beta2*age[i]
  }
  tau   ~  dgamma(0.01, 0.01)
  beta1 ~  dnorm(0, 0.0000001)
  beta2 ~  dnorm(0, 0.0000001)
})

consts   <- list(n=n,age=age)
data     <- list(mass=mass)
inits    <- function(){list(beta1=rnorm(1),beta2=rnorm(1),tau=10)}
samples  <- nimbleMCMC(model_string, data = data, inits = inits,
                       constants=consts,
                       monitors = c("beta1", "beta2"),
                       samplesAsCodaMCMC=TRUE,WAIC=FALSE,
                       niter = 30000, nburnin = 10000, nchains = 2)

messages.subject: How to sample from a GMRF
messages.subject_clean: How to sample from a GMRF
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
In a spatial model, the random effect can be interpreted as a Gaussian Markov Random Field (Rue, H and Leonhard H. 2005), given a precision matrix Q from a Leroux model, how is it possible to sample the random effect from the GMRF?
The book proposes the following steps

I try to write it:

code <- nimbleCode({
  for(k in 1:Area){
    O[k]~dpois(b[k])
    log(b[k])<-log(E[k])+mu+phi[k]
    RR[k]<-exp(mu+phi[k]) }

  #Leroux.Struct
  Q<-((1-rho)*diag(Area))+(rho*W)
  Leroux.Struct[1:44,1:44]<-chol(Q)
  phi[1:Area]<-solve(t(Leroux.Struct), Z)

  # priors
  mu~dnorm(0,0.0001)
  rho ~ dunif(0, 1)
  tau~dgamma(0.01,0.01)
})

But in this case, the parameter Z  is fix to a single value (Z<-mvrnorm(1, mu=rep(0,44), Sigma=diag(44))) which does not make sense to me because it will not be an iterative process.

Thank you in advance
--
Diego

Rue, Havard, and Leonhard Held. Gaussian Markov random fields: theory and applications. CRC press, 2005.

Hi Chris, when it says "undefined reference" in your previous message,
it seems to not be finding C++ functions and classes that should be
present in files in
C:\Users\chjennel\Documents\R\win-library\4.0\nimble\include\nimble,
even though the "-I" flag should be telling the compiler to look
there.

Can you list out the files (and their sizes) in
C:\Users\chjennel\Documents\R\win-library\4.0\nimble\include\nimble,
and in your response show what those are? I'm wondering if those files
are messed up somehow.

Chris

messages.subject: Re: How to sample from a GMRF
messages.subject_clean: How to sample from a GMRF
messages.body_plain:
You need to specify "Z" as being stochastic in the model declaration
in your call to modelCode(), such as:

for(i in 1:44)
  Z[i] ~ dnorm(0,1)

That's the prior that corresponds to the generative model in the
algorithm you cite. 'Z' needs to be a parameter in the model that is
sampled via the MCMC.

A more computationally efficient implementation for the matrix
computations, which avoids the full matrix inverse of 'solve', is
this:

Q[1:44,1:44] <-((1-rho)*diag(Area))+(rho*W[1:44,1:44])
 Leroux.Struct[1:44,1:44]<-chol(Q[1:44,1:44])
phi[1:Area] <- backsolve(Leroux.Struct[1:44,1:44], Z[1:44])

(And note that I've included full indexing of all vectors and matrices.)

I'll also note that CAR models (as implemented in nimble with
dcar_normal and dcar_proper) are a special case of GMRFs, so those
might be of use to you.

Finally I'll note that nimble won't take advantage of sparsity in Q
(this is on our long-term to-do list), so for larger models, the
computation won't scale well.

-Chris

> Dear all,
> In a spatial model, the random effect can be interpreted as a Gaussian Markov Random Field (Rue, H and Leonhard H. 2005), given a precision matrix Q from a Leroux model, how is it possible to sample the random effect from the GMRF?
> The book proposes the following steps
>

>
> code <- nimbleCode({
>   for(k in 1:Area){
>     O[k]~dpois(b[k])

>     RR[k]<-exp(mu+phi[k]) }
>
>   #Leroux.Struct
>   Q<-((1-rho)*diag(Area))+(rho*W)
>   Leroux.Struct[1:44,1:44]<-chol(Q)
>   phi[1:Area]<-solve(t(Leroux.Struct), Z)
>
>   # priors

>   rho ~ dunif(0, 1)

> })
>

> Thank you in advance

On Thursday, June 21, 2018 at 12:19:40 AM UTC-6, pdevalpine wrote:

> Dear Matt,
>
> Thanks for the question.  I can't reproduce your example without your data file (nrow(LagTemp) is the first hurdle), but I think I see the issue.
>
> Especially in model code, nimble's hard typing can be confusing when one is used to dynamic type conversions in R.  In this case, matrix multiplication returns a matrix (as it does in R), and dl.effect[d,a] is a scalar (it is a length-1 vector in R).  In R, the assignment from a 1x1 matrix into a non-matrix is automatically converted due to *run-time* checking of the matrix size.  In nimble, all types are determined at compile time (as in C++), so you need to tell nimble that you know the matrix will be in effect a scalar.  A way to do so would be:
>
>  dl.effect[d,a] <- (Temps[d,1:(L+1)]%*%(DLBasis[((a-1)*(L+1)+1):((a-1)*(L+1)+1+L),1:n.DLBasis]%*%beta.DL[1:n.DLBasis]))[1,1]
>
> The previous question on the list was also about the friction of scalar <--> non-scalar conversions.  It's something we hope to make smoother in future renovations, although maybe we should try to put together shorter-term accommodations.
>
> Perry
>
>

> On Thu, Jun 21, 2018 at 5:40 AM Matthew Heaton <matth...@gmail.com> wrote:

messages.body_plain:
There are three cpp files (each with a .cpp and .h) compiled for a model and MCMC, two for the model, one for the MCMC.  It looks like the C++ compiler is found but there are errors that look like linking errors.

I think the failure to find the final dll that you copied is the last downstream manifestation of earlier compilation errors, which look like linking errors.

These are, unfortunately, difficult problems for us to diagnose in that they seem to be system-specific, unless there is some change associated with Rtools40 that we need to learn about.

Can I suggest a few experiments (each separate):

Try installing nimble from source: install.packages("nimble", type = "source")

Be sure your R session has administrative privileges.

Try using "dirName = 'some_local_dir'" in your calls to compileNimble.  (You will have to switch from using nimbleMCMC to building and compiling the model and MCMC directly, with nimbleModel -> buildMCMC -> compileNimble.  However the problem might manifest just from compiling the model, without an MCMC involved.)

Try installing nimble in a local directory (lib argument to install.packages, then lib.loc argument to library).

-Perry

Thabnk you Perry - I will try your suggestions. After trying the first one, installing Nimble from 'source', I get the following error/warning:

> install.packages("nimble", type = "source")

Error in install.packages : Updating loaded packages

Restarting R session...

Loading required package: nimble
Error in .requirePackage(package) :
  unable to find required package ‘nimble’
In addition: Warning message:
In library(package, lib.loc = lib.loc, character.only = TRUE, logical.return = TRUE,  :
  there is no package called ‘nimble’

On Wednesday, April 29, 2020 at 6:17:16 PM UTC-5, pdevalpine wrote:

> There are three cpp files (each with a .cpp and .h) compiled for a model and MCMC, two for the model, one for the MCMC.  It looks like the C++ compiler is found but there are errors that look like linking errors.
>
> I think the failure to find the final dll that you copied is the last downstream manifestation of earlier compilation errors, which look like linking errors.
>
> These are, unfortunately, difficult problems for us to diagnose in that they seem to be system-specific, unless there is some change associated with Rtools40 that we need to learn about.
>
> Can I suggest a few experiments (each separate):
>
> Try installing nimble from source: install.packages("nimble", type = "source")
>
> Be sure your R session has administrative privileges.
>
> Try using "dirName = 'some_local_dir'" in your calls to compileNimble.  (You will have to switch from using nimbleMCMC to building and compiling the model and MCMC directly, with nimbleModel -> buildMCMC -> compileNimble.  However the problem might manifest just from compiling the model, without an MCMC involved.)
>
> Try installing nimble in a local directory (lib argument to install.packages, then lib.loc argument to library).
>
> -Perry
